leads.title: Egan v. Canada, [1995] - Supreme Court of Canada
leads.documents: Landmark ruling that sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under s.15 equality clause of the Canadian Charter as an analogous ground; foundation for LGBTQ anti-discrimination protection applicable in Quebec.
leads.detail: Cited in text as 'Egan v Canada' 1995 landmark decision; s.15(1) Charter equality clause

leads.title: Vriend v Alberta, [1998] - Supreme Court of Canada
leads.documents: Held failure of a provincial legislature to include sexual orientation in human rights law is itself a s.15 Charter violation; led to all provinces/territories and federal government explicitly including sexual orientation and gender identity by 2017.
leads.detail: Cited as 'Vriend v Alberta' 1998 decision; noted as basis for human-rights-act coverage

leads.title: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms - Section 15(1), Section 1 (Oakes Test), Section 33
leads.documents: Constitutional rights machinery: s.15 equality guarantee, s.1 reasonable limits test, s.33 notwithstanding clause; governs enforcement against laws and law-enforcement authorities across Canada including Quebec.
leads.detail: Quoted s.15(1) text in article; Constitution Act 1982, in force 1985; Oakes Test; s.33 five-year exemption discussion

leads.title: National Assembly of Quebec - 2002 Amendments to the Civil Code of Quebec creating civil unions
leads.documents: Quebec-specific relationship recognition: created legal status of civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples with same effects as marriage re family direction, parental authority, family residence/patrimony; valid only in Quebec.
leads.detail: Cited as 2002 National Assembly amended Civil Code of Quebec; conjoints de fait vs civil union spouses distinction

leads.title: Quebec court ruling declaring Criminal Code s.159 unconstitutional
leads.documents: Quebec component of multi-province invalidation of discriminatory anal-intercourse provision (s.159) as violation of Charter equality; documents decriminalization enforcement history in Quebec.
leads.detail: Cited as 'courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and Alberta each independently declared section 159 to be unconstitutional'

leads.title: Civil Marriage Act (Federal, 2005)
leads.documents: Federal law legalizing same-sex marriage nationwide; followed Supreme Court Reference re Same-Sex Marriage (Dec 2004) confirming federal jurisdiction; applies in Quebec.
leads.detail: Cited as Parliament passed bill on July 20, 2005; Canada fourth country worldwide, first in Americas; Supreme Court Dec 2004 reference

leads.title: Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150)
leads.documents: Federal decriminalization of same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults, in force upon royal assent June 27, 1969; initiated by Justice Minister Pierre Trudeau.
leads.detail: Cited as Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 also known as Bill C-150; brought into force June 27, 1969

leads.title: Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act (2018)
leads.documents: Federal remedial law allowing persons convicted of pre-1969 homosexual acts or s.159 anal intercourse to have RCMP/federal and notified provincial/municipal police/court records destroyed/removed; expungement vs pardon distinction.
leads.detail: French title: Loi sur la radiation de condamnations constituant des injustices historiques; royal assent June 21, 2018; Parole Board of Canada explanation cited

leads.title: Bill C-32 / Bill C-75 - Repeal of Criminal Code s.159 (Royal Assent June 21, 2019)
leads.documents: Repeal legislation setting age of consent for anal intercourse to 16, equalizing with other sexual activity; government stated s.159 was archaic legislation affecting young men.
leads.detail: Cited as Bill C-32 introduced Nov 15, 2016 incorporated into Bill C-75 tabled late March 2018; royal assent June 21, 2019; statement by MP Randy Boissonnault special advisor on LGBTQ2 issues

leads.title: Privy Council Office-commissioned poll (2020) on social acceptance
leads.documents: Government institutional survey documenting public attitudes relevant to visitor safety: 91.8% comfortable if neighbour gay/lesbian/bisexual and 87.6% comfortable if neighbour transgender person.
leads.detail: Cited as 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office; also cites 2020 Pew Research 85% favoured acceptance
